Make The Team / product design review

The same team.
A more considered app.

A review of the screens and features that grew around the original design, with a practical proposal for making them feel like one product.

6 September 2026 · Baseline: IA and screens, committed 20 August · Guide evidence + source review at 70286df
VerdictBaselineFindingsProposed screensDesign rulesDeliveryCoverage
01 / Overall assessment

The brand survived. The hierarchy did not scale.

The app does not need a new visual identity. It needs clearer boundaries between reading, deciding and managing. New features mostly inherit the colours and fonts, but too often arrive as another heading, another form and another large button.

Keep

Warmth and clarity

The cream ground, expressive headings, plain language and generous response buttons are distinctive and appropriate for a weekly social game.

Fix

Competing tasks

Team assignment, settings, results and account utilities need their own hierarchy. Equal visual weight makes every feature demand attention at once.

Avoid

A cosmetic reskin

More cards, icons or tighter spacing alone will not solve this. Preserve the fast player journey and organise complexity around the organiser’s actual jobs.

Evidence matters. All 32 guide images were visually inspected. They are useful evidence of the supplied experience, but some predate fixes in the current source. This document labels those differences rather than presenting already-fixed issues as new work. The mockups below are proposals, not screenshots of a running application.
02 / What the original design established

Extend the grammar, not just the palette.

The original HTML explicitly covered response, join, sign-in, dashboard, organiser game and fixture pages, account, admin and email. Team picking, guests and account utilities were already part of that direction; they are not all later inventions. Results, delegated picking, priority invitations, richer notification controls, timeline, season statistics, standings and the later player controls expanded its demands.

03 / Detailed review

Where it feels added rather than designed.

High priority · observed + source

01. Team picking needs to feel like a workspace.

Observed: two empty coloured boxes, a second run of player names with native radio circles, then large neutral actions. The first squad list handles attendance; the next list handles teams. The distinction is logical, but the visual transition is too weak.

Why it feels unfinished: native radios are not inherently bad. Here their loose spacing and default appearance sit beside much more deliberate In/Out segments. Counts, empty drop zones and choices read as separate fragments. Green and peach also borrow the app’s success/warning language for two equally valid sides.

Proposal: restore the original raised Teams panel; place counts in the team headers; use labelled, styled native radio segments; give “not assigned” a clear state. Keep a saveable draft separate from publication, with the readiness reason always visible. Use long team names above the controls and compact labels with full accessible names when necessary.

Current-source caveat: action wrapping and the picker handover disclosure have already improved. Retain those fixes. Do not introduce drag-only assignment or merge Save and Publish.

High priority · observed + source

02. Notification settings look like a small spreadsheet.

Observed: long descriptions share a narrow first column while Email and Push checkboxes float beside them. Timing fields appear within selected rows. The column labels are far above the lower controls; one unavailable channel is a dash.

Impact: reading, channel selection and scheduling compete across the row. The owner must keep the column meaning in memory while scanning several screens. This is a layout problem, not a need for more explanatory copy.

Proposal: each message type gets a title, concise timing summary and locally labelled Email / Push controls. Timing edits expand beneath their message. Group ordinary reminders separately from organiser-only notices. For push-only messages, say “Push only” rather than showing a dead cell.

Keep the explanation that fixtures still open when reminders are off. Preserve the distinction between the result-request notification’s timing and the later result-answer window setting. Do not introduce per-section saves without deciding their server-side scope.

High priority · observed + source

03. Results should lead with the result.

Observed: the provisional score is a compact bordered row. Its Agree action competes with an always-open alternate score form, outcome radios and “Record it”. “1 backer” and “Locks…” sound more like internal mechanics than a friendly post-game task.

Proposal: make the score the visual anchor and label it “Result so far”. Explain the deadline in plain language. Give agreement a specific action label and put alternate entry behind “I remember a different result”. When no result exists, show the entry form immediately.

Do not hide disagreement: show all competing candidates and support counts when they exist. Preserve the viewer’s existing answer, withdrawal and locked/read-only states. If the window elapsed with no claim, follow the actual continued-entry behaviour instead of inventing a locked state.

Finish: reuse the shared field component, with clearly visible score inputs and full-size outcome labels. The current source duplicates field styling in result-specific CSS, which is a maintenance warning as well as a visual one.

Medium priority · observed + source

04. Account history interrupts account maintenance.

Observed: name and sign-in settings are followed by four large fixture cards, then installation, then notifications. A short list pushes device setup far down the page. Two top-level headings split what the original called one “This device” task.

Proposal: name → signing in → this device → concise recent activity → account actions. Combine installation and notification states in one panel. Treat blocked permission as a state with a clear next step, not a generic warning competing with every other account section.

Use compact history rows here, and reserve rich response cards for Games. A complete cross-game history destination would be new work; until it exists, preserve the current history’s access rather than hiding records behind a dead link.

Medium priority · partially addressed

05. The organiser fixture needs a clear route through it.

Observed: attendance, team choices, picker ownership, guest entry, WhatsApp copy and operational links form one long sequence. The white WhatsApp panel attracts more visual attention than the larger Teams task above it.

Proposal: retain the fixture context and urgent capacity state at the top. Add compact anchor navigation for Squad, Teams, Messages and History. Keep attendance visible; frame Teams as a task; open message composition and secondary controls on demand. Use “Add a guest” beside the squad heading as a secondary destination.

Already addressed: source now links to a separate guest page and uses a picker disclosure. Build on that. Do not count their old full forms in the screenshot as remaining implementation defects.

For priority invitations and manual promotion, keep actions next to the relevant player and explain the effect. A place on the waitlist, an invitation and a confirmed place must never share an ambiguous “In” label.

Medium priority · verify after recapture

06. Operational details need words and visual restraint.

Observed: most squad rows show crossed-out device/notification symbols; the timeline repeats full timestamps and tiny details. Neither helps an organiser quickly find the one thing that needs action.

Already addressed: current squad-row signals omit ordinary “not installed/no push” states, and timeline entries are grouped by day with the event title first. These are the right changes, not candidates for a second implementation.

Remaining proposal: check actionable signals on an actual phone. Use visible short text such as “Messages failing” when action is needed, with detailed context on the member page. Screen-reader-only labels do not explain icons to a sighted touch user. Keep history’s back-link predictable and add filters only if realistic event volume justifies them.

05 / A small, enforceable design system

Make future additions easier to get right.

Keep Caprasimo for page titles and major section headings; Figtree for text, form labels and controls. Use expressive type to establish hierarchy, not for every nested tool. Retain the warm palette, but distinguish team identity from success and warning states.

Task surface

Text + colour
Needs attention
Text + colour
PatternProposed ruleAcceptance check
Page shellSigned-in pages start directly below the shared header. Token pages retain their minimal context. Keep one predictable back-link.Short and long pages share the same starting rhythm; long names wrap without moving navigation off-screen.
Spacing & surfacesUse a 4/8/12/16/24/32px scale. Use 24–32px between tasks, 12–16px inside them, and 16–20px card padding. Cards enclose tasks; rules separate list rows.A reader can name each task without reading its form fields. Avoid card-inside-card accumulation.
Action hierarchyPrimary fill for the next committing action in the active task; neutral for reversible edits; text links for navigation; destructive styling only for destructive actions.Save, publish and message links do not look interchangeable. Keep server consequences clear.
Form controlsShare field, segmented choice, checkbox row and error components. Use native inputs with visible labels, deliberate borders and consistent radii.Visible focus, full-label activation and at least 44px proposed touch targets. Result inputs and team choices feel related to the rest of the app.
Status & colourUse words for meaning. Team colours have separate identity tokens; a green side is not “correct” and an amber side is not a warning.Selected team, personal answer, match status and unsaved draft are distinguishable without colour.
DisclosureCollapse secondary tools, not required decisions. Show a useful summary. Open for validation errors, pending handover or an active exception.Keyboard and no-JavaScript use still work; posted values in closed sections survive validation and saving.
FeedbackPlace receipts beside the changed task: “Draft saved. Nobody notified.” Use the actual outcome/channel for publish and message receipts.Do not claim delivery when only queued, or promise email when that channel is off.
Readability requires measurement, not taste. The source already has contrast tests and many 44px controls. This review does not certify accessibility. Check every actual text/background pair at its rendered size, especially small accent text on peach, muted helper copy, field boundaries, selected controls and dark mode. The darker button in these mockups is a proposed treatment, not a request to replace the brand colour everywhere.
06 / Implementation proposal

Consolidate in three reviewable passes.

Pass 1 · Highest value

Finish the core workspaces

Teams panel and choices; result summary and alternate entry; notification rows; combined device panel. Resolve action hierarchy with complete populated states.

Size: medium. Primarily view/CSS work, with meaningful interaction checks.

Pass 2 · Navigation and density

Make long pages navigable

Fixture section anchors, concise history links, compact account history, invitation summaries and touch-friendly standings detail. Separate secondary tasks only where an existing route fits.

Size: medium to large. New destinations or save boundaries need route and product decisions.

Pass 3 · Prevent drift

Capture the states that matter

Refresh guide screenshots and the screen catalogue. Document shared patterns, then review every new feature against them using busy, empty and error states.

Size: small to medium, depending on fixture data coverage.

Where the changes belong

src/views/layout.ts and styles.ts: shared tokens and primitives. team-picker.ts and owner-fixture.ts: task framing and actions. game-form.ts: settings grouping. result.ts: result hierarchy. account.ts and install.ts: account structure. league-table.ts, invite-order.ts, mute-controls.ts and preview-banner.ts: later feature review.

Keep the existing server-rendered forms, separate player/organiser renderers and CSS registration mechanism. Move repeated visual behaviour into shared primitives rather than copying more field declarations into feature-specific styles. Preserve draft versus publish, waitlist versus confirmed place, invitation eligibility, notification preferences and result-lock semantics.

Definition of done

  • Review at 320, 390 and 768px, plus desktop and 200% text zoom; no page-wide horizontal scrolling or clipped actions. Test long names and long team labels.
  • Capture teams unassigned, partially assigned, saved, published and changed after publication; include overcapacity, a guest and a delegated picker.
  • Capture results empty, proposed, disputed, already backed, withdrawn, locked and without an agreed score. Show eligibility differences without misleading inactive forms.
  • Capture settings with channels on/off, priority invitations on/off, validation errors and effective-date notices. Preserve all saved values across disclosures.
  • Capture account install/permission states, zero and multiple devices, no history and long history; test relevant browsers rather than assuming one permission flow.
  • Verify keyboard and touch operation, visible focus, label associations, status announcements, colour contrast and no-JavaScript core flows.
  • Run a short task-based review with organisers and players: assign and publish teams, change reminder timing, agree or dispute a result, pause future attendance, and restore phone notifications. Record hesitation and wrong turns before asserting usability improvements.

Already changed in source: verify, don’t redo

Current code top-aligns signed-in pages, limits squad-row signals to actionable exceptions, groups the timeline by day, collapses picker handover in its ordinary state, and links to a separate guest task. It also contains later mobile standings, response-button and capacity treatments. The screenshots do not consistently show these changes. Fresh captures are the first acceptance gate for implementation, not a reason to ignore the supplied evidence.
